analysis.one_liner: Requires all U.S. electricity to come from renewable sources by 2035 and sets binding greenhouse gas reduction targets.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would direct the Department of Energy to write rules requiring that 100% of electricity sold in the U.S. come from renewable sources by 2035, and to set escalating annual targets for electricity and natural gas savings through 2030. It would also require the EPA to set annual greenhouse gas reduction targets so that U.S. emissions in 2035 are at least 52% below 2005 levels and reach zero by 2050, then write final regulations to meet them. Suppliers could meet the efficiency targets through a market-based trading system.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, the main gains would be long-term: cleaner air, lower exposure to climate-driven disasters like floods, wildfires, and heat waves, and energy-efficiency targets that could reduce household utility bills. Renewable energy and storage businesses would gain a guaranteed growing market, and utility customers would benefit from mandated efficiency investments.

how_it_helps.text: Requires 100% of retail electricity sold in the U.S. to be generated from renewable sources by 2035 and each year after.
Sets cumulative targets requiring retail electricity and natural gas suppliers to achieve end-use efficiency savings each year through 2030, with savings each year added on top of the last.

Requires the EPA to set annual emission reduction targets ensuring U.S. greenhouse gas emissions in 2035 are at least 52% below 2005 levels and zero by 2050, with final implementing regulations within seven years of enactment.
Allows suppliers to meet efficiency targets through a market-based trading system, and preserves the ability of states to adopt stronger renewable or efficiency rules.
Requires periodic National Academies reviews of whether the targets are sufficient to avoid dangerous climate change, with agencies required to act on recommendations or explain why not.

analysis.who_pays: Fossil fuel producers would bear the cost of a shrinking market for oil, coal, and natural gas in power generation. Electric and gas utilities would bear compliance costs for the renewable and efficiency mandates, and any compliance costs could be passed through to customers on their bills. Building the renewable generation and transmission needed for a fully renewable grid by 2035 would require very large near-term capital spending.

drawbacks.text: A 100% renewable electricity requirement by 2035 is an extremely aggressive timeline that would require rapidly replacing most existing generation and building major new transmission; an honest supporter would acknowledge the risk of higher electricity prices and grid-reliability strains if construction cannot keep pace.
The bill would push compliance costs onto utilities and their customers, and its trading systems could let some suppliers buy credits rather than deliver savings directly to households.

The EPA's broad mandate to impose additional requirements 'from any source or sector' to reach net zero by 2050 would sweep in industries well beyond electricity, raising costs in agriculture, transportation, and manufacturing without specifying how.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential long-run benefits — avoiding the worst climate damages and lowering household energy use — are large, and the findings section cites peer-reviewed evidence on the costs of inaction. But the compliance pathway runs through utility bills and a very tight 2035 deadline, so near-term costs to ratepayers and fossil fuel regions would be real and unevenly distributed. The bill is ambitious but offers limited relief mechanisms for households facing the transition.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which sent it to a subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ted Lieu introduced the Climate Solutions Act of 2023 on September 14, 2023, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Environment, Manufacturing, and Critical Materials; no further action, hearing, markup, or vote appears in the bill's history.
Only one Democratic member cosponsored the bill, and no Republican support is recorded.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill died without receiving a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers and utilities that would have faced the renewable, efficiency, and emissions mandates are better off because the bill never advanced; no supplier had to change how it generates or sells energy.

for.name: 1 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no other members signed on during the Congress.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it.

against.name: Subcommittee on Environment, Manufacturing, and Critical Materials
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on September 15, 2023 and took no further action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only Democratic support — a Democratic sponsor and a single Democratic cosponsor — and no Republican backing is recorded; the Republican-controlled House committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill's 100% renewable electricity mandate and economy-wide net-zero-by-2050 target would shrink demand for fossil fuels used in power generation and beyond. In this case the industry's interest ran against a bill whose climate and air-quality benefits flow mainly to the public.

industries.industry: Electric utilities and natural gas suppliers
industries.note: Utilities would bear escalating renewable and efficiency mandates and compliance costs likely passed to ratepayers, but the bill's market-based trading system would let some suppliers profit from selling savings credits rather than investing directly in customers' efficiency.

A guaranteed national renewable standard would create a steadily expanding market for wind, solar, storage, and transmission builders. That interest runs alongside the public's interest in cheaper, cleaner power, though ratepayers would fund the transition through their bills.
